Around it hang four small untitled works on paper.

This is the part of the job that nobody outside the building knows exists. A label looks like a set of facts, and half of it is a decision. We have about sixty words for a room text and about twenty for a label, and every one of them is negotiated. The medium line is where it usually gets difficult. An artist will write, quite reasonably, that the work is a sound piece about a hospital, and we have to turn that into mixed media, four-channel sound, hospital furniture, printed transcripts, because a label describes what is in the room, not what the work is about. What the work is about goes in the room text, and the room text is a different genre entirely. My advice to any artist who is about to be shown for the first time is very simple. Ask to see the label before it is printed, and read the medium line out loud. If it does not sound like your work, say so that week, because once it is on the wall it stays there for the whole run of the show.

A quick word about the two lines at the bottom of the label, the ones visitors skip and researchers read first. The credit line tells you how the work got here. Courtesy of the artist means it came straight from the studio and goes straight back to it. On loan, with a date after it, means it belongs to somebody else and we have it for a fixed period, and when that date passes the wall goes empty until we hang something else. Acquisition, with a year after it, means it is ours and it is not going anywhere. The second line is the provenance, which is the ownership history, and it is only ever as good as the paperwork. For work made in the last ten years it is usually complete. For anything older, or anything made inside an institution like a hospital or a school, there are gaps, and we write attributed to rather than by when we cannot prove the hand. That one word is the difference between a certainty and a strong argument, and it is not a small thing to put on a wall.
It is a four-channel sound installation, not a sculpture.
